title: Why the Supreme Court Threw Out the Bridgegate Convictions
summary:
Why did the Supreme Court throw out the Bridgegate convictions? In 2013, two New Jersey officials cut Fort Lee's access lanes to the George Washington Bridge from three to one behind a fake traffic study — four days of gridlock, starting on the first day of school. A jury convicted Bridget Anne Kelly and Bill Baroni on all seven counts, including wire fraud and federal-program fraud. On May 7, 2020, a unanimous Supreme Court reversed: the scheme showed "deception, corruption, abuse of power," Justice Kagan wrote, but it did not aim to obtain money or property.
Kelly v. United States, from the court record: the "Time for some traffic problems in Fort Lee" e-mail, the traffic-study cover story, the $3,696.09 in toll-collector overtime, the jury's question, the 2016 verdict and sentences, the property-fraud argument, the 9–0 ruling and what came after (Ciminelli, Percoco, Kousisis).
docs_note: Documents shown are a U.S. Department of Justice (Solicitor General) brief, U.S. district court records and Congressional Research Service reports (public domain). Trial transcripts and exhibits are quoted, not shown.
